turns.prompt_text: I'm at goodwill, a pair of rollerskates have 16 ball bearings total, 2 per wheel. There are 4 pairs for $10 each And one for $15
turns.response_html:
That is a solid stash of potential project components. Let's break down exactly what you're looking at in terms of hardware yield and value.

The Breakdown

If every skate follows that formula (16 bearings per pair, 2 per wheel across 8 wheels total), here is what the inventory looks like:

  • The $10 Pairs (4 available): 64 bearings total $\rightarrow$ 15.6¢ per bearing
  • The $15 Pair (1 available): 16 bearings total $\rightarrow$ 93.8¢ per bearing

If you buy out the entire lot for $55, you'll walk away with 80 ball bearings at an average cost of about 68.7¢ each.

Things to Consider Before Buying

Before you drop the cash, it's worth doing a quick inspection right there in the aisle to make sure they are actually usable for your projects:

  • The Standard Size Check: Most standard roller skates use 608 bearings (8mm inner diameter, 22mm outer diameter, 7mm width). This is the absolute gold standard size for 3D printing projects, custom spinners, and small electronics because they fit common M8 hardware perfectly.
  • Shield Type: Check if they have rubber shields (usually marked RS) or metal shields (ZZ). Rubber shields are easier to pop off with a pin if you need to clean out old, gunked-up grease and relubricate them with light machine oil for a freer spin.
  • The Spin Test: Give the wheels a quick flick. If they feel gritty, crunching, or barely move, they might have rusted internal races. If they just feel sluggish, it's likely just old, hardened factory grease, which can be dissolved in an isopropyl alcohol bath.

If they are standard 608s and the metal isn't rusted through, grabbing a couple of the $10 pairs is a incredibly cheap way to stock a hardware bin.

Those are graphite or charcoal sketching sticks, used for drawing, shading, and architectural or creative sketching.

The markings on them give away exactly how they perform:

  • 6B: A very soft, dark graphite. It goes down smoothly, blends easily, and is perfect for deep shadows.
  • 2H: A hard graphite. It leaves a much lighter, crisp line and is typically used for initial drafting, technical drawing, or fine detail work because it holds its edge well and doesn't smudge easily.

The rest of the sticks in that tray likely span the gradient between those two extremes (from soft/dark "B" grades to hard/light "H" grades, with "HB" right in the middle).

If they are priced cheaply like the skates, they are a fantastic pickup for quick design mockups, whiteboard-style planning on paper, or shading large areas quickly without wearing down a standard pencil.
